items.title: What exploited vulnerabilities have in common: A data-driven analysis of real-world attacks
items.detail: In this article Classifying the vulnerability landscape Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Impact, exposure and where to focus Next in line How Microsoft Security helps defenders act References Learn More The vulnerability landscape continues to expand. From 1999 through September 2026, approximately 383,000 software vulnerabilities had been disclosed across platforms and technologies, yet only about 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. Those vulnerabilities follow clear patterns. Threat actors disproportionately target flaws that enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploit development could further shorten the window defenders have to respond. Patching remains essential, but remediation can take weeks or months on critical systems, and some legacy or unsupported systems cannot be patched. Defenders therefore need to concentrate protection where it can have the greatest impact, considering both the likelihood of exploitation and the potential blast radius of a successful attack. Classifying the vulnerability landscape To make this large vulnerability population actionable, we analyzed each CVE across two dimensions: impact class and affected platform. Impact class captures the outcome a threat actor could achieve by exploiting a vulnerability. Each CVE is assigned to the most consequential impact it directly enables. For example, when a vulnerability can bypass authentication and directly enable remote code execution (RCE), we classify it as RCE. This approach helps distinguish the underlying type of vulnerability from the security impact an attacker could achieve. Server-side RCE: Remote code execution on a network-exposed service without user interaction. Client-side RCE: Remote code execution that requires a user to open or run malicious content. Local code execution: Code or command execution requiring local access or an existing foothold. Local privilege escalation: Elevation from lower-level access to SYSTEM or root privileges. Authentication or authorization bypass: Circumvention of authentication or access controls. Security-control bypass: Circumvention of protections such as sandboxing, secure boot, or SmartScreen. Information disclosure: Exposure of sensitive data or secrets. Tampering or integrity: Unauthorized modification of data or system state. Denial of service: Disruption of system or service availability. Cross-site scripting (XSS): Script execution within a victim’s browser context. Arbitrary file access: Unauthorized access to or placement of files. Spoofing or redirect: Spoofing, redirection, or other forms of UI deception. We also classified vulnerabilities by the platforms they affect, including Windows, Linux/Unix, mobile, network appliances, IoT/OT, virtualization hosts, and developer packages. A CVE can span multiple platforms. Developer packages are treated as a separate category because they are often cross-platform and represent a significant share of the overall vulnerability population. Most CVEs in the analysis affect application code, including servers, web applications, browsers, productivity software, libraries, and firmware tooling, while a smaller share affects OS and system code such as kernels, drivers, and firmware. This analysis covers CVEs published through September 2026 using Microsoft’s catalog of tracked vulnerabilities. Each CVE is counted once in the impact analysis and across each relevant platform in the platform analysis. Figure 1 – The full published-CVE population as of September 2026, broken down by impact class and affected platform, and an OS vs. application split. Breadth dominates – many impact classes spread across many platforms, with about 77% of CVEs in application code and 23% in OS/system code. Vulnerabilities exploited in the wild The subset of vulnerabilities exploited in the wild is much smaller than the overall CVE population, and looks very different from it. Fewer than 1 in 200 published CVEs are ever used in a real attack, and those that do get used are overwhelmingly concentrated in the takeover classes that maximize threat actor impact and exposure. The difference becomes clear when we look at impact. Exploitation is heavily concentrated in vulnerabilities that give attackers greater control over a system. Server-side RCE rises from 20% of published CVEs to 37% of exploited CVEs, local privilege escalation from 11% to 18%, and client-side RCE from 4% to 13%. By comparison, XSS falls from 15% to 4% and denial of service from 16% to 7%. OS vulnerabilities show a similar shift, increasing from 23% of the overall CVE population to 41% of exploited vulnerabilities. These patterns are consistent with threat actors favoring vulnerabilities that can provide meaningful access and control. Remote code execution and privilege escalation can create footholds that support subsequent stages of an attack, while vulnerabilities that primarily cause a crash or limited script execution may offer less utility for broader compromise. Importantly, a vulnerability’s stated classification does not always reflect what an attacker can reliably achieve in practice. For example, some vulnerabilities described as enabling RCE may ultimately result only in denial of service under real-world conditions. Understanding the demonstrated impact and exploitability of a vulnerability is therefore critical to effective prioritization. Figure 2 – The 2,056 exploited-in-the-wild CVEs distribution, compared against the full published population: ghost lines mark each class and platform’s share of all ~380K published CVEs, and badges show the shift in percentage points. Takeover classes and OS code rise, while high-volume XSS and DoS fall. Where defenders should focus Patching is slow, while exploitation is fast Patching is slow, and far slower on critical systems than others. Across platforms, servers are the critical assets and the slowest to patch. Microsoft Security Exposure Management data from 2026 shows that the median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers. It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on MacOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor’s window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest. Exploitation runs on the opposite clock: the most impactful vulnerabilities are weaponized in days, increasingly on or before disclosure. According to VulnCheck , 29% of the exploits in 2025 were launched within 1 day of CVE publication. According to CISA, the mean time from CVE publication to CISA KEV catalog fell from 89 days in 2024 to 57 days in 2025. 2026 data up to September already have that number dropping to 20 days, with a median of only 3 days since publication. Industry research suggests that advances in AI are a significant factor in the time reduction required to develop exploits, further increasing pressure on defenders to respond quickly. Impact, exposure and where to focus Two things determine a vulnerability’s value to a threat actor: impact and exposure. Impact is what successful exploitation provides, such as remote code execution or privilege escalation. Exposure is an asset’s position in the environment and the opportunities it creates for further compromise. An asset’s exposure is shaped by the identities, privileges, and connections available from it. Servers often use service accounts, application identities, or cloud-managed identities with permissions beyond their operational needs. Compromising such a system can provide access to additional resources, sensitive data, administrative privileges, or trusted network paths. Together, impact and exposure determine the blast radius: a vulnerability that enables full control of a highly exposed system can enable widespread on-premises or cloud compromise. Threat actors do not exploit at random: they go after the vulnerabilities that give the highest impact and exposure: full control of a system and the privileged identities and critical assets it has access to. As defenders, focusing on these vulnerabilities first can deliver the highest return on remediation investment. Takeover vulnerabilities like remote code execution, authentication bypass and local privilege escalation lead here. They drive the broadest exposure and the largest blast radius, account for 78% of real-world exploited vulnerabilities, and stopping their exploitation interrupts attacks at the earliest stage, before compromise can propagate across the environment. Next in line A second slice deserves attention where context makes it severe: denial of service against availability-critical assets is recoverable in general, but can be mission-ending in parts of your environment where uptime is everything; disclosure of credentials or secrets can be minor as an insulated incident, but it feeds the same privileged-identity path mentioned above. Figure 3 – The three remote-takeover classes analyzed across 1,239 exploited CVEs), each drilled down by affected platform and split into OS vs Application code. Bar length is the CVE count per platform; the dark segment is OS/system, the light segment is application. How Microsoft Security helps defenders act Threat actors do not begin with a vulnerability list. They begin by looking for a reachable way in. Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management approaches the environment from that same outside-in perspective, continuously discovering internet-facing infrastructure, including previously unknown or unmonitored assets, shadow IT, and third-party dependencies. This gives defenders an opportunity to remove unnecessary exposure before a reachable vulnerability becomes an entry point. Once the reachable assets are known, the next question is which weaknesses deserve immediate attention. Defenders need a way to prioritize exposure beyond CVSS alone. Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management addresses this challenge through Exposure Score and prioritized security recommendations . Prioritization incorporates threat and exploitability signals, breach likelihood, internet exposure, and asset criticality, helping teams focus remediation on vulnerabilities that create the greatest actual exposure. An initial foothold is only part of the risk. Attack Path Analysis connects assets and threat actor techniques into end-to-end routes from an entry point to a critical asset. Microsoft Security Exposure Management Attack Path Analysis provides a cross-workload view spanning endpoints, cloud, and hybrid environments, using vulnerability context from MDVM, endpoint data from Defender for Endpoint, and cloud asset data from Defender for Cloud. Within cloud environments, Defender CSPM Attack Path Analysis adds detailed context about internet exposure, vulnerabilities, network connections, identities, and permissions across Azure, AWS, and Google Cloud. Together, these experiences show how an exposed workload could become a path through a privileged identity to sensitive data or another critical resource, helping defenders identify where to break the path before the initial compromise expands. Patching remains essential, but it is not the only defensive action available. Microsoft Security helps defenders discover the doors threat actors can see, prioritize the weaknesses they are most likely to exploit, understand where a compromise could lead, and identify opportunities to break attack paths before compromise spreads to critical assets. items.title: Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet
items.detail: Introduction Last week, Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor which enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM). Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates’ malware modules onto infected devices. These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices. We also took action to disrupt the command and control (C2) domains that operate these affiliate modules. Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. We found this malicious software built directly into many different device models and brands over multiple years, supported by dedicated infrastructure and constantly evolving configurations to evade detection and manage their affiliates. We believe this campaign wasn’t an isolated rogue insider or a development oversight. As a result, Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned them from making devices with preloaded Google apps. Google requires OEMs go through a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to ensure a consistent and safe user experience across the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong employed obfuscation techniques to exploit a gap in our tests and load malicious code after the device's first boot. As a result, Google has implemented changes to its existing review process to better safeguard against similar activity in the future. A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust, and represents a serious risk to those users. Without users’ knowledge or consent, infected devices were offered as a distribution mechanism for a wide array of criminal actors. This led to a variety of malicious activities being conducted on and through the devices, including ad-fraud, data exfiltration, and routing malicious network traffic through the devices. We worked closely with Japan’s National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI to analyze this malware ecosystem and disrupt its operations. While we expect this disruption to have a significant effect on these criminal operations, this is not the end of our work combatting malicious activity. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain. Point-in-time disruptions are a critical tool to protect our users, but lasting disruption in this fluid ecosystem will require continued targeting of this infrastructure. Google undertook the following actions to support disruption of the XCPE botnet: Legal action to take down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet and install malware modules Legal action to take down C2 domains used by over a dozen malware families loaded as modules via this backdoor Banned Videostrong and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices in the future, or supplying software to other certified vendors Implementing improvements to how we ensure the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices Overview The x.cpe network was built for ongoing profit. By giving malware affiliates backdoor access, the operators conspired to monetize these devices long after purchase. Figure 1: XCPE malware overview Malware Since at least late 2024, Videostrong has evolved its pre-installed malware from simple single-stage droppers into a modular, three-stage architecture designed for resilience and multi-tenant monetization: Primary Backdoor: Operating at the android.uid.system privilege level, x.cpe (running as com.oemservice in some builds) is preloaded in the firmware partition. If uninstalled by a user, it automatically reinstalls from the /oem/ partition upon reboot, maintaining persistent system-level access. Its main function is to establish and facilitate communications between the C2 server and the loader and execution engine. Loader and Execution Engine: To evade security scans, x.cpe acts primarily as the C2 communicator and offloads module execution to an external loader, com.abc.nexus . This file employs native anti-analysis utilities to thwart sandbox detection, and configures and initializes the monetization modules. Most recently, com.abc.nexus has itself been phased out in favor of using more tailored dropper malware that loads and executes single modules. Monetization Modules: Videostrong monetizes its backdoored devices by loading monetization modules which are developed by entities other than Videostrong that act as affiliates. These modules are deployed as native ELF daemons, embedded SDKs compiled directly into the com.abc.nexus DEX bytecode, or are fetched as secondary APKs from the malware staging infrastructure. The loaded modules transform infected devices into residential proxy exit nodes (e.g., Linkfog, AppSalt, NetNut), ad-fraud engines (e.g., CBOXTV, HiddenView), or execute additional backdoors that load even more monetization modules (e.g. Moyu, Spirit). Infrastructure Command and Control: The botnet uses a two-stage C2 process. It first initiates HTTP POST requests to fetch dynamic configuration settings, geolocation data, and STUN server parameters. It then establishes a persistent, real-time Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) connection to receive instructions for silent app installations, arbitrary shell commands, screen captures, and network reconnaissance. MQTT is a lightweight, publish-and-subscribe network protocol designed for low-bandwidth, high-latency, or unreliable remote networks. Malware staging infrastructure: Additional monetization modules as well as various shell scripts and legitimate applications are hosted remotely and downloaded by infected devices upon command from the operator via the MQTT broker. A significant majority of these files are hosted as Github releases on operator-owned Github pages. Other files are hosted on operator-controlled servers and file hosting sites. Malware Deep Dive Backdoor Initialization The infection chain begins with a stub package (called x.cpe in some builds and com.oemservice in others) preloaded in the system partition of the firmware and running at the android.uid.system privilege level. This stub has limited functionality. Upon boot, it checks the device's oem/ directory for the corresponding x.cpe package and initiates installation into the /data/app/ directory as outlined below. To maintain inter-process state across the firmware ecosystem, x.cpe exports two ContentProviders, which expose structured configuration tables storing runtime parameters, device identifiers, proxy configuration blobs, and execution flags accessible by co-installed system applications. This enables other apps in Videostrong’s ecosystem, such as their YokaTV Player streaming software, to fetch configuration parameters provided by the C2 server mentioned below. C2 Configuration The malware utilizes a two-stage communications protocol. It first fetches initial bootstrap configurations via an HTTP request, followed by a persistent MQTT subscription to receive commands and module download instructions. To dynamically derive the HTTP C2 bootstrap server, it follows the following routine: Queries content://com.release.debug.provider/configs for private_url via x.cpe.util.ExtraReadUtils . Queries the Android system property to determine if ro.mecool.device is true. If true, it defaults to http://mcstb.anyevonline.com:8000 If false, it dynamically generates the following: http://stb[AndroidVersion][Type].anyevonline.com:8000 . Using the selected hostname, the client makes an HTTP POST request with an AES-encrypted JSON object containing hardware telemetry (SN, MAC, model, firmware version) to the following endpoints: /router/config/mqtt : This endpoint provides MQTT broker details (including Broker Hostname, TCP Port, Authentication Tokens/Passwords, and the specific Topic structure: /device/{model}/{chipId}/{action} . After receiving this data, the device initiates a persistent, real-time socket connection to the MQTT broker. /router/config/acs : This endpoint response returns URLs for ip-api[.]com and a Google STUN server to enable the malware to identify geolocation and public IP and port mapping to traverse network address translation (NAT) boundaries. It also returns a URL ( http://ott.szbboys[.]com:8000/cpe/file/upload for uploading files, logs, or diagnostic dumps from the device, and returns flags to configure ad modules ( adBwmActive , adDevourUse , adDevourCode ), and to enable or disable core malware modules. /router/config/app : This endpoint provides module-level configs, including server mappings and parameters, which x.cpe decrypts and passes to a SQLite ContentProvider named ShareProvider ( com.oem.share.provider ). By exposing this inter-process data interface, x.cpe enables modules to retrieve up-to-date upstream infrastructure parameters (such as URLs for additional configs, user manuals, etc). MQTT Capabilities Following initial configuration, persistent real-time C2 communication is managed by the MQTT library ( x.cpe.mqtt.MqttUtils ). All identified samples analyzed to date utilize a single broker hostname, mqtt.szbboys[.]com . Specific MQTT topics are mapped to specific actions, including: Silent Application Installation : Fetches remote APKs to a temporary directory. Disable Google Play Protect : To bypass security, AppUtils.disablePackageVerify() targets the global setting " package_verifier_user_consent " via Settings.Global.putInt and sets it to -1 , disabling Google Play Protect app verification. Arbitrary Shell Execution : Executes remote commands via sh under system UID privilege level. Results are published to the MQTT broker. Shell Script Execution : Downloads and executes shell scripts via x.cpe.util.RunCmds . Remote Desktop Monitor & Screen Capture : Utilizes android.app.Instrumentation.sendKeyDownUpSync() to inject keycodes and Java reflection on hidden APIs ( android.view.SurfaceControl.screenshot / SurfaceControl$ScreenshotHardwareBuffer ) to continuously capture the screen, compress to JPEG, and publish over MQTT. Network Reconnaissance : Invokes embedded binaries ( libtraceroute.so ) to fingerprint the victim network, and perform standard ping tests. The binaries also perform robust AS-lookup WHOIS routing queries. Our analysis of the C2 data indicates the preponderance of interactions with victim devices were related to module install, uninstall, and configuration actions. We also observed Videostrong operators executing sensitive actions on the device, including capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive data including account information, device information, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including to establish reverse shells on devices. Loader and Execution Engine Details Earlier versions of x.cpe directly embedded malicious monetization modules. In late 2024 – possibly as a response to earlier Google enforcement related to BadBox – Videostrong removed malicious modules from x.cpe and introduced a separate malicious package they developed, com.abc.nexus , which x.cpe routes instructions and data to via Inter-Process Communication (IPC). Modern variants of x.cpe facilitate C2 communications but pass configuration parameters, module updates, and other payloads to com.abc.nexus as the execution engine. We believe the actor may have evolved the malware in this way in an attempt to ensure x.cpe could remain undetected. Upon boot, com.abc.nexus.broadcast.BootReceiver broadcasts the com.abc.nexus.data intent, bootstrapping com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . Within CoreService.onCreate , the application performs maintenance and persistence tasks. The main logic sets up a listener through RemoteMessageHandler for IPC communications from x.cpe, and parses JSON payloads received from it. After these steps, CoreService initializes the monetization modules. com.abc.nexus services extract and orchestrate a series of nested native libraries and dynamically downloaded secondary payloads which vary significantly based on sample. Many versions of com.abc.nexus come preloaded with four or more embedded modules, while other versions contain as few as one. The most common malware modules include TitanService , BwmService , AdtimeService , lb102Service , and LinkfogService (sometimes called AgentService) . Discussion of these and other modules can be found in the monetization modules section. Persistence and Evasion The malware operators implement a number of mechanisms to establish persistence and thwart detection and analysis. As a system preload, x.cpe cannot be removed by the user. If x.cpe is uninstalled from /data/app/ , upon reboot the x.cpe service BootReceiver follows the same routine outlined above and reinstalls the package. The backdoor is able to silently download additional files to the device and execute them without user consent because it first wipes user consent configuration on the device and then disables Google Play Protect: public static void disablePackageVerify() { PreferenceUtils.setPackageVerifyFromUser(CPEApp.instance, true); AppUtils.setPackageVerify(-1); // Actioning a bypass against GPP evaluation } Figure 2: Disabling Google Play Protect In many variants of com.abc.nexus, we observed the extraction of a sophisticated anti-analysis and process hardening utility libseccomp_guard.so , which runs prior to the initialization of malware modules, to ensure they remain protected from automated sandboxes and security instrumentation. It filters system calls to prevent the pausing or termination of individual threads, denies cross-process interference to ensure isolation, and prevents the spawning of child processes. Evolution Since August 2026, new dropper packages have been installed via the MQTT channel, which appear to be synchronized with the mass-uninstallation of com.abc.nexus across the botnet. We assess this may represent a new evolution of the malware to further evade detection. These new packages are disguised as Android system applications, with names such as com.android.system.ntp and com.android.sso.auth.handler . Where com.abc.nexus could act as a general purpose loader and execution engine (executing instructions passed to it from x.cpe ), these packages instead install single monetization modules (such as AppSalt). Multiple variants of these packages extract a native ELF file, libexploit.so , which in turn executes functions nativeAdbRoot() and nativeAdbShell() . These functions restart the local adbd service as root, and initiate an ADB shell connection. Following this, the app uses the connection to install itself in the system partition. The system partition is remounted as read-write and the payload replicates itself to a newly minted directory in /system/priv-app/ and creates an XML file at /system/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-<app name>.xml . This file grants the malware android.permission.INSTALL_PACKAGES and android.permission.REBOOT . The app configures the malware modules through hardcoded configuration parameters, and does not listen for x.cpe IPC messages. The app itself is controlled by the operators via shell scripts pushed via the broker and executed by x.cpe . These include setting the property persist.networkstack.uninstall (which, when read by the app, triggers uninstallation and cleanup), persist.networkstack.skip_system_install (which skips system installation, forcing it to remain running in /data/app/ ), and persist.networkstack.install_time (which implements timestomping, overriding the default timestamp of the app to align with the other packages installed in the system directory). Botnet composition The botnet is globally dispersed, with certain concentrations possibly implying market penetration for the brand distributor. Figure 3: Global distribution of x.cpe While the overwhelming majority of the infected devices in the XCPE botnet are Android TV set-top boxes, we observed a number of other infected Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth devices, karaoke machines, and digital signage devices. Monetization x.cpe loads a variety of malicious modules for monetization. Most often the modules are associated with residential proxy services and bandwidth sharing, but we've also observed ad fraud modules. Given that a single device may be running multiple modules providing the same or similar functionality (e.g., as many as three residential proxy SDKs installed on a single device) it is clear that Videostrong seeks to monetize every infected device to the greatest extent possible. Services are loaded by com.abc.nexus via three methods: Native Daemons : Native ELF binaries prepackaged with com.abc.nexus , which are unpacked to data directories and spawned as background processes with system/root privileges. Embedded SDKs / Services : Java/Kotlin SDKs compiled directly into Nexus and invoked via Android Service lifecycles or IPC broadcast triggers. Dynamic Droppers & Secondary APK Installers : Downloader function that pulls remote native ELFs or secondary standalone APKs and invokes system package managers. Nexus receives messages from x.cpe directing it to download specific modules. Malware modules loaded via the backdoor include the following: Residential Proxy / Bandwidth Sharing Modules LINKFOG Com.abc.nexus ’s LinkfogService unpacks a Go binary named lw_android_agent from assets/ to local app storage and supplies it with vendor parameters. This service silently turns infected devices into residential edge computing and PCDN proxy exit nodes. It connects to FRP reverse tunnels, and uploads bandwidth accounting metrics to Linkfog API backends. Linkfog (operated by Beijing Linkfog Technology via 点心云 / Dianxinyun) brands itself as a “Peer-to-Peer Content Delivery Network”. Jaguar The com.abc.nexus AdtimeService extracts libjaguar.so from assets/ . The file is an unobfuscated 32-bit ELF binary written in C, compiled as a native Android binary. It utilizes JNI (Java Native Interface) to initialize its core routines, dynamically derives a ChaCha20 decryption key via ARM NEON SIMD instructions to decode heavily obfuscated configurations , and establishes an encrypted C2 channel. Upon successful registration, the C2 responds with JSON configuration specifying proxy endpoints. The proxy command loop x_ctrl_do_ctrl_msg delegates proxy operations based on incoming JSON variable commands, and is capable of both TCP and UDP relay. AppSalt / Honeygain AppSalt SDK is the residential proxy SDK owned by Honeygain, which is in turn owned by Oxylabs. com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService initializes Appsalt SDK. First, the application obtains an Appsalt SDK API key from a native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getAppsaltKey() function. Appsalt SDK is initialized without displaying a consent screen - instead it explicitly calls the optIn() method which sets a consent flag without displaying any user interface. During Appsalt SDK startup it checks the application's installation source and stops execution if the application was installed from the official Google Play Store. Once Appsalt is successfully initialized it establishes a WebSocket connection with the primary command and control domain. Appsalt uses JSON-formatted messages for initial check-in (registration) and heartbeat requests. Appsalt command and control servers use MessagePack formatted messages to issue commands pertaining to proxy operations. Appsalt SDK is configured with an initial set of domains that act as proxy gateways. The list of proxy gateways can be updated by the command and control server. The device establishes UDP / QUIC connections with these gateways. BWM / IPWeb This residential proxy and bandwidth-sharing node is implemented through the com.abc.nexus.service.BwmService component (sometimes named com.abc.nexus.service.SN4Service) and its associated SDK. Upon initialization, it secures itself within an isolated sandbox environment, captures device telemetry, and registers with a remote server over UDP. From this C2, it receives instructions to initiate a Java NIO TCP multiplexed proxy tunnel. The service functions to route arbitrary traffic through the infected device on behalf of a remote threat actor. GaGaNode GaGaNode is the first-party SDK owned by residential proxy operator IPCola. It connects over TCP to a primary C2 server and sends heartbeat beacon data over HTTP POST to a separate server. The SDK both contains its own proxy relay functionality, and it initializes additional proxy SDKs from affiliates. Upon device registration to the C2, com.gaganode.sdk.node.endpoint.a receives incoming packets from relay servers and places them in queue for the client to read and proxy through its exit node socket. The service manages multiple proxy sessions at once (referred to as clients), and each client has its own tcp/udp queue for messages. We observe GaGaNode initializing PopaNet/NetNut and EarnFM Fleet residential proxy SDKs. GaGaNode/IPCola is thus likely able to further monetize its SDK and offer these affiliates access to the infected exit nodes. NetNut / Popanet Popanet is a residential proxy SDK developed by NetNut, a residential proxy operator. The GaGaNode module initiates the Popanet SDK ( io.popanet.Popa ). This malware is identical to the malware described in our previous disruption of NetNut . All C2 infrastructure used by Popanet samples connected to x.cpe was taken down as part of the earlier Netnut disruption. Traffmonetizer The Traffmonetizer SDK is initialized inside the primary background service com.abc.nexus.service.CoreService . CoreService operation depends on the availability of policy JSON provided by the XCPE backdoor via IPC. Before calling Traffmonetizer SDK initialization methods, the application obtains a Traffmonetizer SDK API key from the native library libnative_keys.so by calling its getTraffmonetizerKey() function. Traffmonetizer functionality is split between two components where the Android SDK acts as a state machine which handles native library callbacks through asynchronous event dispatchers. ServiceBloc monitors connection status updates from the native callbacks and ConnectivityBloc monitors Wi-Fi and mobile data network changes. Traffmonetizer native library initialization and configuration is followed by a call to baseClientStart() which establishes a WebSocket connection to a C2 server. Traffmonetizer uses a single WebSocket (TLS) connection to the command and control server to multiplex control messages and tunneled connections (supports both TCP and UDP). Traffmonetizer also supports “Content Delivery” tunneling which allows nodes to tunnel bandwidth-intensive traffic. EarnFM EarnFM is a residential proxy provider, and Fleet SDK is the provider’s SDK that enrolls devices as exit nodes into the proxy network. In com.abc.nexus , FleetSDK is initialized by com.gaganode.sdk as mentioned above. FleetSdk then loads native binary libfleetshare.so . FleetSDK establishes a persistent WebSocket connection with its primary C2 server for routing arbitrary network traffic. Incoming tasking frames are received over the WebSocket channel and processed in a continuous loop. Messages contain structured JSON commands instructing the daemon to connect to specific remote hosts, with support for both TCP and UDP. Backdoor Modules Spirit Spirit is a dynamic code loading backdoor. Spirit employs multiple stages. The first stage payload fetches device information (hardware, operating system, and manufacturer/brand information and geolocation), posting it over HTTP to a hardcoded C2 server, and fetches a list of additional modules to download from the server. The second stage communicates with a separate server, and is used for tasking, config sync, module retrieval, heartbeats, and reporting. We have observed Spirit loading a significant amount of additional malware monetization modules, including some of the families already directly loaded by com.abc.nexus . Moyu Moyu is a 3-stage backdoor previously observed as part of the BadBox enterprise. On x.cpe -backdoored devices, we observed it initialized by com.abc.nexus.service.DevourService. The first stage is an offline dropper that reconstructs and loads an embedded second stage. Stage two polls an update C2 to download, decrypt, and load the third stage. Stage three implements a backdoor with hidden Double-WebView click/conversion fraud, persistent clipboard hijacking, and secondary dynamically loaded JAR execution and a separate residential proxy trojan. Bird Bird is a 2-stage backdoor previously tied to the BadBox enterprise. Stage 1 beacons a device and analysis-environment profile to its C2 server and, when the server approves, downloads, decrypts, and loads the Stage 2 JAR. Stage 2 implements a dynamic code loading backdoor (two plugin loaders plus a C2-driven reflective method invoker), a separate downloader (silent APK installation and Accessibility-driven Google Play installs), and ad abuse (lockscreen ads, overlays, browser launches). Fission Fission is a dynamic code loading (DCL) backdoor embedded within standard video applications (e.g., com.newtv.cboxtv ). Upon initialization, the first stage plugin contacts its C2 server to download additional modules. The decrypted second stage payload fetches execution targets and tracking URLs from the C2. The request sends an unencrypted POST request with tracking metrics from the internal DeviceManager. The payload we observed was configured to commit ad fraud. Rather than rendering visible advertisements in a WebView or UI component, the Stage 2 plugin executes headlessly in the background. The module queries ad server endpoints in the background to retrieve ad placement responses, parses out both primary impression beacons ( pvm ) and third-party tracking monitor URLs ( pvtpm ), and immediately fires HTTP GET requests to each tracking endpoint to register a fake ad view without displaying creative content. When executing inside specific smart-TV application stores ( com.changhong.appstore or com.tcl.appmarket2 ), the plugin initializes and triggers the ad SDK directly to report synthetic ad exposures. It is a standalone ad fraud application capable of running in the background using a transparent window overlay, using hidden WebViews to load targeted web pages and simulate user interaction (scrolling, clicking, typing, media playback), playing media unattended, and capturing the user’s screen. Call to Action While we believe our actions have seriously impacted over a dozen malicious actors, the underlying illicit market is resilient. Backdoor operators, ad-fraud rings, and residential proxy providers operate as an interconnected supply chain, and when one component is disrupted, operators quickly pivot to new loaders or rival monetization SDKs. Creating lasting change requires accountability across the hardware supply chain, the residential proxy industry, and the broader technology ecosystem. Accountability and Reform A device manufacturer intentionally infecting their users with malware is an unacceptable breach of trust. By turning everyday hardware into persistent beachheads for criminal affiliates, Videostrong prioritized illicit post-sale recurring revenue over the safety and privacy of its users. Downstream hardware brands, white-label resellers, telecommunications providers, and online e-commerce marketplaces also share responsibility for closing this vector. Retailers and distributors should require independent security audits from Original Design Manufacturers (ODMs) and swiftly delist manufacturers implicated in supply-chain abuse. Residential proxy providers have been able to flourish under the guise of legitimate businesses. While some providers may claim to behave ethically and only enroll devices with the clear consent of consumers, any claims of "ethical sourcing" must be backed by transparent, auditable proof of user consent. In our analysis, these proxy operators only seek consent when they are forced due to platform policy and enforcement. Silent opt-in without user consent remains the most prevalent means by which devices are turned into exit nodes. Empowering and Protecting the Consumer Residential proxies are an understudied area of risk for consumers, and more can be done to raise awareness. Consumers should be extremely wary of applications that offer payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your internet." These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device’s home network. We urge users to stick to app stores you trust, review permissions for third-party VPNs and proxies, and ensure built-in security protections like Google Play Protect are active. Consumers should only purchase connected devices, such as set-top boxes, from reputable manufacturers. Our Android TV website provides the most up-to-date list of partners. Industry Collaboration We encourage mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces and other tech platforms to continue sharing intelligence and implementing best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software and limit their harms. items.title: The Rise of LLMJacking: How Threat Actors Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources
items.detail: Written by: Christopher Romano, Codi Starks, Garrett Mahoney, John Wolfram, Josh Murchie, K Singh, Mathew Potaczek, Mike Lombardi, Rik Dolfing Introduction Mandiant responded to multiple incidents in 2026 in which threat actors hijacked enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs), a tactic known as "LLMJacking." Spanning a variety of cloud and LLM providers, these intrusions impacted organizations in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours. Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked. Figure 1: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests Analyzing the criminal ecosystem behind these frontline compromises, and building upon previous reporting on the growing underground market for LLM credentials, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) has identified a diverse set of financially motivated threat clusters operating out of multiple regions globally. As the LLMJacking ecosystem matures, we are also tracking a division of labor between threat actors establishing initial access to compromised environments and operators managing downstream monetization infrastructure, known as “LLM Mixers”. LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to underground subscribers. In one investigation, GTIG observed two distinct operational clusters coordinating to compromise and monetize enterprise LLM infrastructure, demonstrating the sophisticated specialization emerging in this space. In this blog post, we describe the attack lifecycle observed across recent LLMJacking investigations and provide actionable detection, hardening, and remediation guidance to help organizations secure their infrastructure. Initial Access While low-level resource theft has involved the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation, threat actors conducting LLMJacking bypass these front-end interfaces to target backend model resources directly. Specifically, they focus on either identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM application programming interface (API) keys. An example of the latter can be seen in Figure 1, where a threat actor uses an automated script to verify exposure by calling the /api/create endpoint to independently run their own models on endpoints that unsuspecting users have left publicly accessible. Leaving these services unprotected not only expands an organization's traditional attack surface, but could also introduce a significant increase in hosting costs. Figure 2: Threat Actor tests publicly exposed Ollama endpoints and attempts to register their own models Across multiple LLMJacking investigations, however, the dominant initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens—including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs), and active session tokens—which threat actors leverage to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure. For instance, in mid-2026 UNC6993 compromised a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used this access to grant further access to an LLM API. UNC6993 also hosted a session hijacking page masquerading as an application portal to join a group of LLM users. This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multifactor authentication (MFA) controls. In another instance, one threat actor gained initial entry by combining a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) to access private code repositories with the exploitation of a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment. Similarly, a different threat actor leveraged compromised IAM credentials of corporate users, using cloud federation tokens to programmatically generate fresh access keys to circumvent MFA requirements. In a separate incident, a threat actor was first observed accessing the environment with a compromised cloud Service Account key with broad project permissions. Beyond general cloud identity credentials, threat actors also target LLM API keys. For example, a threat actor opportunistically harvested exposed corporate LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories. Demonstrating advanced evasion tradecraft, the group conducted automated credential validation sweeps using minimal single-token requests ( max_tokens=1 ). This allowed the threat actor to stealthily confirm the viability of the stolen keys while remaining undetected by the victim’s endpoint detection and response (EDR) and SIEM volume anomaly alerts. Lateral Movement and Persistence After gaining an initial foothold, threat actors systematically work to escalate privileges, solidify access, and conduct internal reconnaissance to identify targets and further cloud credentials. To expand their access, threat actors enumerated cloud services, code repositories, and data stores for sensitive credentials. In one intrusion, a threat actor conducted internal reconnaissance across multiple cloud regions to map available services and identity policies. In a separate intrusion, a threat actor compromised a containerized cloud environment. Once inside, they performed extensive repository reconnaissance, cloning sensitive codebases to search for hardcoded secrets, configuration variables, and developer credentials. They also scanned access logs to identify credentials for secondary cloud environments. Threat actors also executed targeted database queries to harvest additional credentials; in one case, the threat actor queried cloud data warehouse metadata tables to search for database credentials, administrator passwords, and sensitive columns, alongside performing cloud object storage operations associated with targeted data theft. Across intrusions, we observed threat actors abusing cloud identity permissions and virtual machine configurations to escalate privileges and maintain persistent access. Utilizing service accounts associated with compromised workloads, one threat actor exploited token-creation privileges to generate temporary credentials for high-privilege service accounts, resulting in the exfiltration of infrastructure credentials, internal database passwords, and third-party API keys from cloud secret managers. Other threat actors established persistence by creating unauthorized IAM and service accounts and injecting SSH keys into compute instances. Specifically, one actor escalated privileges by attaching administrative policies to service roles, created unauthorized IAM accounts with full administrative rights, and established interactive management sessions into running virtual machines to inject unauthorized SSH public keys into host configuration files. Similarly, another threat actor created deceptive backdoor service accounts disguised as internal billing optimization utilities and injected environment-wide SSH keys into compute instance metadata. Beyond exploiting traditional cloud infrastructure permissions, we have observed instances of threat actors targeting vulnerabilities specifically within LLM routing software to escalate privileges. In one case, after acquiring pre-validated Virtual Keys from the threat actor that established initial access, a follow-on cluster executed targeted application logic exploitation against the victim's LiteLLM gateway. The actor exploited a user ID rebind vulnerability in the /key/regenerate endpoint (CVE-2026-40217) to elevate standard Virtual Keys into full PROXY_ADMIN master administrative credentials, establishing deep, persistent control over the compromised environment. LLM Abuse The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning. Threat actors frequently enabled a variety of managed generative platforms, and created additional API keys to scale their operations. Upon acquiring LLM API access keys, UNC6993 attempted to generate additional API keys and enable associated services within victim cloud projects, quickly accumulating over $100,000 USD in billing charges. Another threat actor subscribed victim accounts to Pay-As-You-Go agreements, selecting premium foundation models and launching high-volume inference streams. To bypass rate limits, the threat actor deployed a "burn and rotate" strategy, continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts while auditing the cloud provider’s billing interface to monitor financial impact. Threat actors also leveraged their access to host their own proxy endpoints and agentic workloads. For example, one threat actor enabled agents, deployed publicly accessible reverse proxies, and used custom Node.js proxy bundles to expose endpoints compatible with multiple frontier LLMs rebranded under a persona known as D1337-KAIROS . The actor deployed a containerized backdoor using the Manus agent framework to the compromised cloud environment, which queried an upstream LLM to reason through instructions and execute resulting commands locally, supported by SearXNG metasearch and agent-infra/sandbox execution environments. To scale compute, the threat actor provisioned compute instances with powerful GPUs, attempted to spin up high-end hardware across multiple regions, and requested quota increases via the cloud provider’s API. The actor also hosted LiteLLM gateways on external servers to manage and route API traffic. Rather than consuming hijacked compute solely for their own operations, GTIG observed evidence of threat actors monetizing compromised API quotas by selling access to these resources through LLM Mixers. The threat actors used open-source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure to pool stolen credentials, meter usage, and obscure the origin of the requests. For example, UNC6993 used open-source tools such as new-api (a centralized model hub and gateway) and gcli2api (an API proxy tool converting command line interface (CLI) tools into standard frontier model endpoints), likely to aggregate stolen keys and balance request loads across accounts. We believe the threat actor sells access to these tools via underground storefronts. Another threat actor that executed more than 500,000 LLM API calls in less than eight hours leveraged stolen third-party API keys to power the token routing service jet-night.com . Jet Night passed nearly one million dollars in token costs to the victim organization. Given Jet Night’s per-token costs to users are so far below typical market rates GTIG believes the service relies on stolen keys to operate profitably. For example, Jet Night offers an unlimited token plan for approximately $60 USD per month with alleged access to frontier models, a consumer service level that would typically run between $100 and $250 per month. Moreover, the service has advertised multiple outages on its public Telegram channel which is likely due to stolen keys being revoked as victims discover their respective compromises. Figure 3: Screenshot of Jet Night Plans and Pricing Structure A threat actor deployed custom proxy relay infrastructure ( ai-relay ) hosted on deceptive lookalike domains. For example, they registered a domain to masquerade as the victim's legitimate internal host. This custom relay infrastructure was used to seamlessly siphon high-value commercial LLM access into the illicit newapi[.]pro resale ecosystem, directly draining the victim's corporate account quotas to serve their underground customers. Outlook GTIG expects that threat actors will increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking, driven by the immediate, high-margin monetization enabled by emerging underground LLM Mixers. As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware. This operational specialization will sustain a growing illicit resale marketplace, allowing threat actors to rapidly siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected. Detection and Hunting In the event that security measures have failed, it is critical that defenders have early visibility into abuse of cloud LLM platforms. Defenders should prioritize detection of modifications to LLM accounts and services and treat any unauthorized enablement as a critical security event. In multiple incidents that Mandiant investigated, LLM services were not enabled at the time of compromise. Abuse of access keys allowed the threat actor to modify and enable LLM API services (e.g. Bedrock, Gemini API, etc.). Once enabled, the threat actor can use the APIs to generate massive bills to the organization in just minutes or hours. Google Security Operations Google Security Operations customers have access to these broad category rules and more under the Cloud Threats, Mandiant Frontline Threats, Mandiant Hunting Rules rule packs. The activity discussed in the blog post is detected in Google SecOps under the rule names: AWS Account Key Creation AWS Create New Access Key AWS Create User Account AWS Delete User Account Base64 Encoded Shell Command Execution Create and Delete Firewall in Default Network GCE Project SSH Keys GCP Service Account Key Creation GCP Create New Service Account GCP Firewall Rule Created Linux Archive Exfiltration via Curl or Wget Persistence: Compute Set Instance or Project Metadata Startup Scripts or URLs Mitigation and Remediation To prevent attackers from abusing Cloud LLM services, defenders should prioritize Identity and Access Management (IAM) and supply chain security, two of the most common pathways for gaining access to and abusing Cloud services. Credential Hygiene : Utilize a centralized secrets management platform to control the management and rotation of sensitive keys and secrets. Automation of secrets and keys can limit the lifespan of leaked credentials. Least Privilege : Ensure users and service accounts only possess the permissions necessary for their specific role and required tasks. Deny all permissions that are not explicitly required, including access to Cloud LLM services. Code Monitoring : Automate secret scanning within codebases (GitHub, Gitlab, etc.) to ensure API keys and secrets added to source code are identified and removed promptly. Routine Configuration Audits : Perform periodic comprehensive configuration audits of Cloud services to identify potential attack paths and unintended exposure of endpoints. Rate Limiting : Implement a WAF like Google’s Cloud Armor to enforce rate limiting for individual client connections. Network Allow Listing : Restrict outbound connections from Cloud services via VPC firewall rules to known IP addresses where feasible. Budget Alerts : Implement granular API quotas on LLM services to limit request volume per model. Utilize spending caps to set budgets and avoid over-spending. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA): Enforce phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication across all cloud identity providers, management consoles, and developer platforms to ensure that stolen credentials or session tokens cannot be easily exploited. Shadow LLM Discovery: Utilize Security Posture Management tools to automatically scan your hybrid cloud environments and identify unauthorized or unmonitored tools, models, and infrastructure, ensuring complete visibility of your model footprint. Granular API Key Scopes: Restrict and segment API keys by specific model endpoints, environments (dev/prod), and usage limits to ensure a compromised token for a basic utility model cannot be used to invoke expensive, high-tier frontier models. Validation Sweep Monitoring: Monitor model gateway and API access logs for anomalous, low-volume requests (such as max_tokens=1 or zero-temperature pings). Attackers frequently use these micro-transactions for stealthy credential validation sweeps prior to launching large-scale infrastructure abuse. Vulnerability & ML Supply Chain Patching: Integrate automated vulnerability scanning (SAST/DAST/SCA) across your custom application code, containerized workloads, and machine learning dependencies (like PyTorch and Hugging Face libraries) to prevent initial access via unpatched server vulnerabilities. Gateway Patch Management: Extend vulnerability management programs to include centralized model proxy and routing gateways (e.g., LiteLLM), ensuring rapid patching against privilege escalation and authentication bypass flaws (such as CVE-2026-40217). Sandboxed Execution for Dynamic Workloads: Isolate the runtime environment in highly virtualized, process-isolated, serverless sandboxes if your LLM application is required to execute generated code or database queries dynamically. Vetted Model Repositories: Restrict and enforce model pulls and pipeline dependencies solely from trusted internal registries or approved enterprise catalogs to prevent developers from pulling compromised models containing pre-configured backdoors. Graph-Based Exposure Modeling: Implement continuous, graph-based risk prioritization that maps cloud assets, application code, and data flows to automatically identify and remediate complex, multi-hop attack paths. Adversarial Exposure Validation: Deploy automated offensive agents to continuously test external attack surfaces, uncover exposed endpoints, and simulate credential validation sweeps. Monitoring Native Cloud Audit Logs AWS : Monitor CloudTrail logs for API events from bedrock.amazonaws.com . Based on historical LLM Jacking incidents, monitor for the following API operations across the attack lifecycle: Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM via the Converse , InvokeModel, and InvokeModelWithResponseStream API operations. API Throttling & Error Spikes: Monitor for high-volume spikes in ThrottlingException , ValidationException , or ResourceNotFoundException errors, which could indicate an automated “spraying” methodology targeting cloud infrastructure. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity used to discover available models via the ListFoundationModels,ListInferenceProfiles , and GetFoundationModelAvailability operations. Additionally, monitor for attempts to unlock new models in the environment via the PutUseCaseForModelAccess and CreateFoundationModelAgreement API operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view, alter, or disable logging configurations to conceal prompt contents and avoid detection. Monitor the GetModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration operation, as well as PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration and DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration . Any calls to disable logging by non-IaC (Infrastructure as Code) principals should be treated as high severity. Automated Tooling: Analyze User-Agent strings to identify automated tools and SDKs (e.g., claude-cli, aws-sdk-rust, and aws-sdk-go-v2) interacting directly with the target cloud infrastructure. Azure : Monitor Azure Activity Logs (Control Plane) and Diagnostic Logs (Data Plane) for events associated with the Microsoft.CognitiveServices namespace. To hunt for or detect LLM Jacking incidents, monitor the following operations: Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM. In Azure, model invocations occur on the data plane and require Diagnostic Logs to be enabled. Look for high volumes of POST requests to inference endpoints such as Completions or Chat Completions APIs. On the management plane (Activity Logs), monitor for unauthorized creation of new instances via the Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write operation. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity to discover available Azure LLM resources, models, and deployments via the Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/read and Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/read operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view or modify logging configurations (to see if data plane model invocations are being recorded) via the Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/read , Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/write , or Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings/delete operations. GCP : Monitor Cloud Audit Logging for calls to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform endpoints (aiplatform.googleapis.com). Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform inference operations are contained within Data Access logs, which are disabled by default due to volume and ingestion costs. You must manually configure your IAM audit policies to track these. Enablement of Agent Platform Services : Alert on enablement of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform services via the google.api.serviceusage.v1.ServiceUsage.EnableService method. Resource Exploitation : Monitor for direct execution of the LLM via Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, which requires Data Access audit logging to be enabled. Look for google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.Predict , google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.GenerateContent , and google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PredictionService.StreamGenerateContent operations. Target Scoping : Monitor potential reconnaissance activity to discover available models and endpoints via the google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.ModelService.ListModels , google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.EndpointService.ListEndpoints , and google.cloud.aiplatform.v1.PublisherModelService.ListPublisherModels API operations. Security/Evasion : Review attempts to view or alter logging and audit configurations. Monitor for operations like google.iam.v1.IAMPolicy.GetIamPolicy (to check if Data Access logs are enabled on the project/resource) or attempts to review log exports via google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.ListSinks and google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.GetSink . Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) To assist the wider community in hunting and identifying activity outlined in this blog post, we have included indicators of compromise (IOCs) in a GTI Collection for registered users.
